claim: Tight junctions (TJs) between blood-brain barrier (BBB) endothelial cells construct a robust physical barrier, whose damage underlies BBB dysfunctions related to several neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Tight junctions (TJs) between blood-brain barrier (BBB) endothelial cells construct a robust physical barrier, whose damage underlies BBB dysfunctions related to several neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established knowledge in the field about TJ function and disease relevance.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy (dSTORM) reveals sparse (occludin) vs. clustered (ZO1/claudin-5) molecular architecture of BBB TJs.
source: Nano-scale resolution revealed sparse (occludin) vs. clustered (ZO1/claudin-5) molecular architecture.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data presented in the manuscript showing different organizational patterns of TJ proteins.

claim: In mouse development, permeable TJs become first restrictive to large molecules, and only later to small molecules.
source: In mouse development, permeable TJs become first restrictive to large molecules, and only later to small molecules, with claudin-5 proteins arrangement compacting during this maturation process.
evidence: This claim is supported by tracer experiments at different developmental stages (E12, E16, P9) showing differential size selectivity.

claim: Claudin-5 protein arrangement compacts during TJ maturation process.
source: In mouse development, permeable TJs become first restrictive to large molecules, and only later to small molecules, with claudin-5 proteins arrangement compacting during this maturation process.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis showing increased density of claudin-5 clusters during maturation.

claim: ZO1 clustering is independent of claudin-5 in vivo.
source: Mechanistically, we reveal that ZO1 clustering is independent of claudin-5 in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging of claudin-5 null mice showing unchanged ZO1 clustering organization.

claim: In the developmental context, total levels of claudin-5 inversely correlate with TJ functionality.
source: In contrast to accepted knowledge, we found that in the developmental context, total levels of claudin-5 inversely correlate with TJ functionality.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification showing higher claudin-5 levels at E12 (permeable) compared to P9 (restrictive).

claim: The BBB was identified when dye/tracer injected into the blood circulation reached the majority of body tissues but failed to penetrate the brain.
source: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) was identified when dye/tracer injected into the blood circulation reached the majority of body tissues but failed to penetrate the brain (Hagan and Ben-Zvi, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cells (ECs) were identified as the core component of the mammalian BBB when electron microscopy (EM) allowed imaging of fine ultra-structural cell-biology components of BBB cells.
source: Endothelial cells (ECs) were identified as the core component of the mammalian BBB when electron microscopy (EM) allowed imaging of fine ultra-structural cell-biology components of BBB cells (Brightman and Reese, 1969; Reese and Karnovsky, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to seminal EM studies.

claim: BBB ECs lack fenestrations (openings traversing the entire cell width).
source: Horseradish-peroxidase (HRP) used as an EM compatible tracer revealed that BBB ECs lack fenestrations (openings traversing the entire cell width) and exhibit extremely low rates of transcytosis (vesicular transport), both mediating intracellular permeability in peripheral ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to HRP-EM studies.

claim: BBB ECs exhibit extremely low rates of transcytosis (vesicular transport).
source: Horseradish-peroxidase (HRP) used as an EM compatible tracer revealed that BBB ECs lack fenestrations (openings traversing the entire cell width) and exhibit extremely low rates of transcytosis (vesicular transport), both mediating intracellular permeability in peripheral ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to HRP-EM studies.

claim: Tight junctions (TJs) between neighboring ECs are responsible for intercellular restrictive barrier properties.
source: A central discovery of these studies was that tight junctions (TJs) between neighboring ECs are responsible for intercellular restrictive barrier properties (Brightman and Reese, 1969; Reese and Karnovsky, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: TJs modulation is explored as means to enhance brain drug delivery.
source: Ever since, BBB TJs became a major focus of the BBB research field; TJs modulation is explored as means to enhance brain drug delivery, and TJs damage is investigated to better understand underlying BBB dysfunctions implicated in diseases (neurodegenerative, neuro-inflammatory, trauma etc. [Bauer et al., 2014; Greene et al., 2018; Hagan and Ben-Zvi, 2015; Kealy et al., 2020; Knowland et al., 2014; Liebner et al., 2018; Sweeney et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015; Zlokovic, 2008]).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research in the field.

claim: TJs damage is investigated to better understand underlying BBB dysfunctions implicated in diseases (neurodegenerative, neuro-inflammatory, trauma etc.).
source: Ever since, BBB TJs became a major focus of the BBB research field; TJs modulation is explored as means to enhance brain drug delivery, and TJs damage is investigated to better understand underlying BBB dysfunctions implicated in diseases (neurodegenerative, neuro-inflammatory, trauma etc. [Bauer et al., 2014; Greene et al., 2018; Hagan and Ben-Zvi, 2015; Kealy et al., 2020; Knowland et al., 2014; Liebner et al., 2018; Sweeney et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015; Zlokovic, 2008]).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research in the field.

claim: Several gene families encoding integral membrane proteins (e.g. occludin, junctional adhesion molecules [JAMs], claudins, and tricellulins [LSR/Marveld]) participate in constructing BBB TJs.
source: Several gene families encoding integral membrane proteins (e.g. occludin, junctional adhesion molecules [JAMs], claudins, and tricellulins [LSR/Marveld]) and adaptors that link TJs to the cytoskeleton (such as zonula occludens [ZO]), participate in constructing BBB TJs (Bauer et al., 2014; Furuse et al., 1998; Furuse et al., 1993; Haseloff et al., 2015; Knowland et al., 2014; Langen et al., 2019; Martìn-Padura et al., 1998; Morita et al., 1999; Nitta et al., 2003; Sohet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying TJ components.

claim: Adaptors that link TJs to the cytoskeleton (such as zonula occludens [ZO]) participate in constructing BBB TJs.
source: Several gene families encoding integral membrane proteins (e.g. occludin, junctional adhesion molecules [JAMs], claudins, and tricellulins [LSR/Marveld]) and adaptors that link TJs to the cytoskeleton (such as zonula occludens [ZO]), participate in constructing BBB TJs (Bauer et al., 2014; Furuse et al., 1998; Furuse et al., 1993; Haseloff et al., 2015; Knowland et al., 2014; Langen et al., 2019; Martìn-Padura et al., 1998; Morita et al., 1999; Nitta et al., 2003; Sohet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying TJ components.

claim: Conventional light microscopy does not enable proper resolution for nano-scale imaging of TJ architecture.
source: Immunofluorescence and imaging with conventional light microscopy provided insights into the molecular components of TJs. Nevertheless, these approaches do not enable proper resolution for nano-scale imaging of TJ architecture.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the resolution limits of conventional microscopy.

claim: Electron microscopy provides superb resolution to image cellular structures but is much less effective in simultaneously localizing multiple proteins and tracer molecules.
source: Electron microscopy on the other hand, provides superb resolution to image cellular structures but is much less effective in simultaneously localizing multiple proteins and tracer molecules, limiting our ability to study the molecular architecture of TJs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the capabilities and limitations of EM.

claim: bEND.3 cells were shown to form TJs in a gradual process that includes translocation of claudin-5 from cytoplasmic and general membrane localizations to the cell boundaries in contact between adjacent cells.
source: These cells were shown to form TJs in a gradual process that includes translocation of claudin-5 from cytoplasmic and general membrane localizations to the cell boundaries in contact between adjacent cells (Koto et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on bEND.3 cells.

claim: During the in vitro maturation process, claudin-5 expression is increased reaching maximal levels by 3 days post-confluence.
source: Previous studies also demonstrated that during this process, claudin-5 expression is increased reaching maximal levels by 3 days post-confluence.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous studies on bEND.3 cells.

claim: The monolayer trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) is elevated reaching maximal levels by 7 days post-confluence in bEND.3 cells.
source: The monolayer trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER), a proxy for TJ function reflecting intercellular restrictive properties, is elevated reaching maximal levels by 7 days post-confluence (Koto et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on bEND.3 cells.

claim: Both claudin-5 and ZO1 are not organized in continuous lines but rather in disrupted lines with discrete clusters, forming bead-like structures.
source: Super-resolution imaging allowed us to demonstrate that both claudin-5 (green) and ZO1 (red) are not organized in continuous lines but rather in disrupted lines with discrete clusters, forming bead-like structures (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: At post-confluence, signals along the membrane were more diffused, forming elongated clusters and ZO1 signals intermingled with claudin-5 signals.
source: A pronounced change was found in the organization of the two TJ proteins at the cell-cell contacts: at post-confluence, signals along the membrane were more diffused, forming elongated clusters and ZO1 signals intermingled with claudin-5 signals (Figure 1b, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: At super-confluence, claudin-5 signals along the membrane became concentrated in more discrete and shorter foci, flanking ZO1 signals.
source: In contrast, at super-confluence, claudin-5 signals along the membrane became concentrated in more discrete and shorter foci, flanking ZO1 signals (Figure 1b, arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Average claudin-5 cluster density was ~4 fold higher at the super-confluence state than in the post-confluence state.
source: Average signal density (per cluster) was also higher at the super-confluence state (~4 fold, Figure 1e, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Total claudin-5 protein levels in bEND.3 cells rise with time in culture.
source: In line with previous publications (Koto et al., 2007), we could confirm that total claudin-5 protein levels in bEND.3 cells rise with time in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: bEND.3 monolayer trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) is relatively low (~40–100 Ωxcm2).
source: Nevertheless, we found that in general, bEND.3 monolayer trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) is relatively low (~40–100 Ωxcm2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEER measurements performed in the study.

claim: Human iPSC differentiation into brain microvascular endothelial-like cells (iBMECs) presents substantially superior barrier features with pronounced TJ function and TEER levels closer to those estimated for the in vivo levels.
source: Therefore, we turned to an alternative in vitro system that presents substantially superior barrier features with pronounced TJ function and TEER levels closer to those estimated for the in vivo levels: human iPSC differentiation into brain microvascular endothelial-like cells (iBMECs) (Lippmann et al., 2014; Lippmann et al., 2012; Vatine et al., 2017; Vatine et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on iBMECs.

claim: In iBMECs, TEER levels started at ~500–1000 Ωxcm2 already a day after seeding.
source: In our culturing conditions, TEER levels started at ~500–1000 Ωxcm2 already a day after seeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEER measurements performed in the study.

claim: Only clustered organization of claudin-5 could be found in iBMECs.
source: STORM imaging revealed that only clustered organization of claudin-5 could be found in these cells (Figure 2c), and that pronounced change in nano-scale organization of claudin-5 clusters could be observed; clusters were smaller in area and denser (Figure 2d–f) along with improvement in TJ function.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Pronounced change in nano-scale organization of claudin-5 clusters could be observed in iBMECs; clusters were smaller in area and denser along with improvement in TJ function.
source: STORM imaging revealed that only clustered organization of claudin-5 could be found in these cells (Figure 2c), and that pronounced change in nano-scale organization of claudin-5 clusters could be observed; clusters were smaller in area and denser (Figure 2d–f) along with improvement in TJ function.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data and quantification shown in Figures 2c-f.

claim: The average signal density (per cluster) was higher with elevated TEER in iBMECs (~2.3 fold).
source: The majority of cluster areas were smaller than 0.1 μm2, and the average signal density (per cluster) was higher with elevated TEER (~2.3 fold, Figure 1f, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Clusters of claudin-5 are much denser in iBMECs compared to bEND.3 cells (~8 fold denser), which correlates with differences in TEER.
source: In general, clusters of claudin-5 are much denser in iBMECs compared to bEND.3 cells (~8 fold denser), which correlates with differences in TEER.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of quantitative dSTORM data between the two cell types.

claim: The in vitro process of TJ maturation is accompanied by TJ nano-architectural changes characterized by the formation of smaller, denser and more discrete clusters of TJ proteins.
source: Altogether, we suggest that the in vitro process of TJ maturation is accompanied by TJ nano-architectural changes characterized by the formation of smaller, denser and more discrete clusters of TJ proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined dSTORM data from both bEND.3 and iBMEC experiments.

claim: Claudin-5 exhibits clustered organization in vivo, demonstrated in both cross and sagittal sections of cortical capillaries.
source: We found that similar to the in vitro data, claudin-5 exhibits clustered organization also in vivo, demonstrated in both cross and sagittal sections of cortical capillaries (of post-natal mice, Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data of brain tissue shown in Figure 4b.

claim: From mouse embryonic day 12 (E12) until E15, the newly formed cortical capillaries have not yet acquired their full restrictive barrier properties.
source: From mouse embryonic day 12 (E12) until E15, we and others have previously shown that the newly formed cortical capillaries have not yet acquired their full restrictive barrier properties (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014; Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on BBB development.

claim: There were about 2.6 times more discrete clusters per capillary at E12 than at P9.
source: Claudin-5 clustering properties analysis showed that there were about 2.6 times more discrete clusters per capillary at E12 than at P9 (657 vs 246 clusters in a set of 20 capillaries of each age, Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Capillary diameter was significantly larger in E12 than in P9 (11.1 ± 0.47 μm and 5.9 ± 0.39 μm, respectively, p < 0.0001).
source: Capillary diameter was also significantly larger in E12 than in P9 (Figure 5a and c; 11.1 ± 0.47 μm and 5.9 ± 0.39 μm, respectively (mean ± s.e.m), p < 0.0001), which might explain the difference in numbers of clusters per capillary.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The total number of claudin-5 signals per capillary was significantly higher in E12 than at P9 (14,341 ± 1257 and 3590 ± 372, respectively, p < 0.0001).
source: In addition to changes in capillary diameter the total number of claudin-5 signals per capillary was significantly higher in E12 than at P9 (14,341 ± 1257 and 3590 ± 372, respectively [mean ± s.e.m], < 0.0001, Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The total cellular amount of claudin-5 is not a strong predictor of TJ functionality in the developmental and early post-natal BBB.
source: Based on this result, we suggest that the total cellular amount of claudin-5 is not a strong predictor of TJ functionality. Our conclusion relates to the developmental and early post-natal BBB (reflected in our data), which might be distinct from the adult BBB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing higher claudin-5 levels at E12 (permeable) compared to P9 (restrictive).

claim: ZO1 has clustered organization in cortical capillaries.
source: Imaging ZO1 and occludin showed that like claudin-5, ZO1 had clustered organization (Figure 6a left), whereas occludin was much less organized in discrete clusters and had more dispersed organization patterns (Figure 6a right).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Occludin was much less organized in discrete clusters and had more dispersed organization patterns in cortical capillaries.
source: Imaging ZO1 and occludin showed that like claudin-5, ZO1 had clustered organization (Figure 6a left), whereas occludin was much less organized in discrete clusters and had more dispersed organization patterns (Figure 6a right).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: ZO1 is known to physically interact with the C-terminals of both claudin-5 and occludin.
source: Based on published biochemical studies, ZO1 is known to physically interact with the C-terminals of both claudin-5 and occludin, which aligns with our imaging data demonstrating signals of all three in close proximity (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to published biochemical studies and imaging data showing co-localization.

claim: Claudin-5 clusters can be detected in close proximity with the lysosomal marker LAMP1, suggesting lysosome localization.
source: Indeed we could detect claudin-5 clusters in close proximity with a lysosomal marker (LAMP1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a), suggesting lysosome localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Claudin-5 clusters can be detected in close proximity with an ER marker (BiP), suggesting ER localization.
source: In addition, we could detect claudin-5 clusters in close proximity with an ER marker (BiP, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a), suggesting ER localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The average density of P9 claudin-5 clusters that were coupled with ZO1 clusters was about five-fold higher than in independent claudin-5 clusters.
source: The average density of P9 claudin-5 clusters that were coupled with ZO1 clusters was about five-fold higher (p < 0.0215) than in independent claudin-5 clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The average density of E12 claudin-5 clusters was similar regardless of proximity to ZO1 clusters, and was low compared to P9 independent claudin-5 clusters.
source: The average density of E12 claudin-5 clusters was similar regardless of proximity to ZO1 clusters, and was low compared to P9 independent claudin-5 clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Claudin-5 clusters in TJs (based on pairing with ZO1) have higher claudin-5 density in late developmental stages, a structural feature that correlates with BBB maturation.
source: We concluded that claudin-5 clusters in TJs (based on pairing with ZO1) have higher claudin-5 density in late developmental stages, a structural feature that correlates with BBB maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the quantitative analysis comparing E12 and P9 claudin-5 cluster densities.

claim: Absence of claudin-5 did not alter ZO1 clustering organization.
source: Finally, we found that absence of claudin-5 did not altered, ZO1 clustering organization nor it had any effect on occludin dispersed organization patterns (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data of claudin-5 null mice shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Absence of claudin-5 had no effect on occludin dispersed organization patterns.
source: Finally, we found that absence of claudin-5 did not altered, ZO1 clustering organization nor it had any effect on occludin dispersed organization patterns (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data of claudin-5 null mice shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The total cellular occludin levels (normalized to capillary circumference) were higher in claudin-5 null capillaries by ~1.29 fold compared to occludin levels in wild-type capillaries.
source: In contrary to the previous conclusions of unaltered molecular composition of claudin-5 null TJs (Nitta et al., 2003), quantification of dSTORM imaging revealed that the total cellular occludin levels (normalized to capillary circumference) were higher in claudin-5 null capillaries by ~1.29 fold compared to occludin levels in wild-type capillaries (P < 0.0039, Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Overall cellular ZO1 expression levels were also higher in claudin-5 null capillaries (not statistically significant).
source: Overall cellular ZO1 expression levels were also higher in claudin-5 null capillaries (not statistically significant).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Nano-scale organization of both ZO1 and occludin are independent of claudin-5 expression (at least in the embryonic setting).
source: We concluded that nano-scale organization of both ZO1 and occludin are independent of claudin-5 expression (at least in the embryonic setting).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dSTORM data of claudin-5 null mice.

claim: E12 capillaries did not restrict movement of tracer molecules across the BBB (10 kDa dextran and ~443 Dalton sulfo-NHS-biotin).
source: As expected from previous experiments with conventional microscopy (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014), with dSTORM imaging we could confirm that E12 capillaries did not restrict movement of tracer molecules across the BBB (Figure 8a; 10 kDa dextran, upper left. ~443 Dalton sulfo-NHS-biotin, lower left).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging of tracer distribution shown in Figure 8a and citation to previous work.

claim: Tracer signals were found intermingled with claudin-5 clusters in E12 capillaries, providing direct evidence of tracer leakage across immature TJs.
source: Moreover, we could directly image TJs contribution to this leakage; tracer signals were found intermingled with claudin-5 clusters (Figure 8, arrows) and in many cases, we could detect tracer signals in three locations relative to claudin-5 clusters: the luminal side, the cluster area itself and the abluminal side. We interpreted these as direct evidence of tracer leakage across immature TJs.
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging of tracer distribution shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Mature P9 capillaries restrict movement of the vast majority of tracer molecules (10 kDa dextran and ~443 Dalton sulfo-NHS-biotin) from the lumen to the basal side.
source: As expected, mature P9 capillaries restrict movement of the vast majority of tracer molecules (Figure 8; 10 kDa dextran, upper right. ~443 Dalton sulfo-NHS-biotin, lower right) from the lumen to the basal side (similar results were obtained using Biocytin, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging of tracer distribution shown in Figure 8a.

claim: E16 cortical capillaries prevent leakage of 10 kDa tracers.
source: E16 cortical capillaries were previously found to prevent leakage of 10 kDa tracers (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014; Licht et al., 2015), also validated here with dSTORM imaging (middle-upper).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging shown in Figure 8a and citations to previous work.

claim: At E16, sulfo-NHS-biotin was not restricted to the vessels' lumen, evident also on the brain side and intermingling with claudin-5 clusters.
source: Surprisingly, at this stage sulfo-NHS-biotin was not restricted to the vessels' lumen, evident also on the brain side (middle-lower arrowheads) and intermingling with claudin-5 clusters (arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by dSTORM imaging of tracer distribution shown in Figure 8a.

claim: BBB TJs might have different maturation time courses for different size selectivity properties.
source: We conclude that BBB TJs might have different maturation time courses for different size selectivity properties and that the dSTORM approach is suitable for in depth investigations of this phenomena in future studies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential tracer permeability observed at E16.

claim: HRP-EM approaches were not useful for studying early embryonic stages of BBB development.
source: We provide direct evidence of non-functional TJs in the early embryonic BBB. HRP-EM approaches were not useful for studying early embryonic stages; consequently direct evidence for the cellular pathway mediating leakage in early embryogenesis was missing.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the limitations of HRP-EM in early embryonic studies.

claim: A recent mouse retina-vasculature study showed that developmentally, the TJ pathway is already restrictive before the vesicular pathway is blocked.
source: A recent mouse retina-vasculature study showed that developmentally, the TJ pathway is already restrictive before the vesicular pathway is blocked (Chow and Gu, 2017) and studies in sheep demonstrated similar trends in the brain (Dziegielewska et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies in sheep demonstrated that the TJ pathway is already restrictive before the vesicular pathway is blocked in the brain.
source: A recent mouse retina-vasculature study showed that developmentally, the TJ pathway is already restrictive before the vesicular pathway is blocked (Chow and Gu, 2017) and studies in sheep demonstrated similar trends in the brain (Dziegielewska et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse cortical vasculature, the course of barrier-genesis might be different from retina and sheep brain.
source: We suggest that in mouse cortical vasculature, the course of barrier-genesis might be different.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential developmental timeline observed in the study compared to other systems.

claim: Even at E16, when vesicular activity is clearly diminished at the BBB, TJs were not fully mature and mediate leakage of a low-molecular-weight tracer.
source: We found that there are different TJ maturation developmental time-courses for different size selectivities. Thus, even in later stages (E16), when vesicular activity is clearly diminished at the BBB (based on ultra-structural EM studies [Bauer et al., 1993]), we found that TJs were not fully mature and mediate leakage of a low-molecular-weight tracer.
evidence: This claim is supported by tracer experiments at E16 and citation to EM studies.

claim: Freeze-fracture EM data suggested cluster organization of EC TJs.
source: TJ claudin-5 shifted into denser cluster organization along with in vivo BBB maturation, a finding which is in line with freeze-fracture EM data that suggested cluster organization of EC TJs (Haseloff et al., 2015; Morita et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous EM studies.

claim: Confocal imaging description of claudin-5 strands might be a misrepresentation of actual claudin-5 organization.
source: Therefore, we suggest that confocal imaging description of claudin-5 strands might be a misrepresentation of actual claudin-5 organization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dSTORM data showing clustered rather than continuous organization.

claim: dSTORM might give rise to some artificial clustering due to antibody staining and fluorophore overcounting.
source: Notably, dSTORM might give rise to some artificial clustering due to antibody staining and fluorophore overcounting (Burgert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on dSTORM limitations.

claim: Previous TJ studies primarily investigated epithelial cells, which have considerably larger volumes than ECs.
source: Previous TJ studies primarily investigated epithelial cells, which have considerably larger volumes than ECs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cell types studied in TJ research.

claim: Previous epithelial TJ studies emphasized a contentious organization of transmembrane proteins along the apical circumference of the cells, providing 'sealing belts'.
source: These studies emphasized a contentious organization of transmembrane proteins along the apical circumference of the cells, providing 'sealing belts'.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous epithelial TJ studies.

claim: The finding of disrupted lines with discrete clusters, forming bead-like structures does not support the concept that claudin-5 fully construct 'sealing belts'.
source: Our finding of disrupted lines with discrete clusters, forming bead-like structures does not support the concept that claudin-5 fully construct these 'sealing belts'.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dSTORM data showing discontinuous claudin-5 organization.

claim: Claudin-5 has huge cellular abundance with an average of ~12,000 transcripts per capillary endothelial cell.
source: Our data supports the huge cellular claudin-5 abundance reported by other approaches (e.g. average of ~12,000 transcripts per capillary endothelial cell Vanlandewijck et al., 2018, average of ~14,000 [E12] or ~3500 [P9] signals per cross section in our data).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to transcriptomic data and comparison to the study's dSTORM data.

claim: Down regulation of junctional protein components are often used as an indicator for TJ dysfunction.
source: Total levels of junctional proteins/transcripts are presented in many studies (measured by western blot, conventional imaging, qPCR/RNAseq etc. [Armulik et al., 2010; Daneman et al., 2010; Nitta et al., 2003; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014]), and down regulation of these components are often used as an indicator for TJ dysfunction (Alvarez et al., 2011; Bell et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2012; Zhong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Claudin-5 expression inversely correlates with BBB tightness in the developmental setting might be distinct from the situation in the adult BBB.
source: Our findings that claudin-5 expression inversely correlates with BBB tightness in the developmental setting might be distinct from the situation in the adult BBB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the developmental data and speculation about adult BBB.

claim: dSTORM imaging of cultured alveolar epithelial cell TJs shows increase claudin-5 in response to alcohol exposure together with an increase in paracellular leak.
source: Similar to our findings, dSTORM imaging of cultured alveolar epithelial cell TJs, shows increase claudin-5 in response to alcohol exposure together with an increase in paracellular leak (Schlingmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The BBB of E18.5 claudin-5 null mouse embryos was hyper-permeable to Hoechst (562 Dalton) and to gadolinium (~742 D) but not to 10 KDa dextran or to endogenous albumin (~66 KDa).
source: The differential size selectivity we found in E16 was reminiscent of the seminal study by Nitta et al., 2003 demonstrating that the BBB of E18.5 claudin-5 null mouse embryos was hyper-permeable to Hoechst (562 Dalton) and to gadolinium (~742 D) but not to 10 KDa dextran or to endogenous albumin (~66 KDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Nitta et al. 2003 study.

claim: Following the Nitta et al. 2003 study, claudin-5 was considered the molecular component of BBB TJs responsible for restricting passage of low molecular weight substances (<800 D).
